title: Sampling and temperature
goals: Sample from a distribution using explicit cumulative intervals
Calculate temperature-adjusted probabilities for a toy example
Explain why random variation and factual reliability need separate evaluation

prerequisite.prompt: Does the largest next-token probability guarantee the largest complete-path probability?
prerequisite.answer: No. Later conditional probabilities can change path rankings, as the two-step counterexample shows.

vocabulary: Selecting an alternative using a specified random procedure
Selecting an alternative with largest next-token probability under a tie rule
A positive parameter that changes the concentration of a distribution under a stated transformation
A range of draws assigned to an alternative using accumulated probability mass

blocks.text: Start with probabilities red 0.6, blue 0.3, green 0.1 in that fixed order. Greedy chooses red. Sampling uses a draw u with 0 <= u < 1 and cumulative intervals: red [0,0.6), blue [0.6,0.9), green [0.9,1). Left endpoints are included, right endpoints excluded. Thus u=0.6 selects blue and u=0.9 selects green. The draw 1 is outside this contract.

Sampling does not mean choosing all tokens equally. Across many independent draws the frequencies may approach the specified probabilities, but a small sample need not match them exactly. Fixed recorded draws allow a reproducible classroom trace. A random seed and generator version help replay a real sampling program, not establish the truth of outputs.

For strictly positive probabilities p_i and temperature T>0, define q_i = p_i^(1/T) / sum_j p_j^(1/T). This classroom formula is equivalent to scaling logits before a softmax when p came from those logits. We use it directly on the supplied table. At T=1 the distribution is unchanged. At T=0.5, square each probability: 0.36,0.09,0.01; total 0.46. The adjusted distribution is red 18/23, blue 9/46, green 1/46.

blocks.title: Keep the evidence roles separate
blocks.caption: Temperature changes probability concentration; the same draw can fall in a different interval.

blocks.text: The lower positive temperature concentrates this table on its largest entry. For T=2, use square roots before normalising; this flattens this unequal distribution. These changes leave the order of positive probabilities unchanged, so greedy still selects red. They change the sampling distribution, not the factual evidence behind a generated claim.

Our formula excludes T=0; dividing by zero is undefined. Some systems offer a zero-temperature setting as a separate greedy policy, but that is not a value to substitute into this formula. We also avoid claiming that any one setting removes all nondeterminism in an unspecified system.

lesson.title: Trace a supported set of draws

blocks.text: Supported draws 0.2,0.6,0.9 at T=1 select red, blue, green. At T=0.5, 0.2 and 0.6 fall below 18/23 and select red; 0.9 lies between 18/23 and 45/46 and selects blue. Keep exact fractions for boundaries, because rounding can misclassify a draw near an endpoint.

blocks.label: Guided: trace those three draws under both distributions and explain why the result is a procedure trace, not a frequency estimate from a large experiment.

lesson.title: Match the experiment to the claim

blocks.text: A fair temperature comparison fixes the prefix, model distribution, candidate order and draw policy. Record multiple outcomes and evaluate task criteria separately. If the aim is creativity in fiction, variation may be useful; if the aim is reporting a sensor state, every factual claim still needs evidence. Never call a probability-concentration change an accuracy improvement without an appropriate evaluation.

blocks.label: Exit: a team lowers temperature and claims hallucinations are impossible. State what was changed and what evidence that claim still lacks.

workbook.title: Trace boundaries
workbook.prompt: At T=1 select tokens for u=0,0.6,0.9 and 0.999. Explain the handling of u=1.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Selections red,blue,green,green. The draw 1 violates the half-open [0,1) input contract and must be rejected.

workbook.title: Compute the adjusted table
workbook.prompt: At T=0.5 compute squared weights, total and normalised probabilities. Check the sum.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Weights 0.36,0.09,0.01 sum 0.46. Probabilities 18/23,9/46,1/46 sum 1.

workbook.title: Compare a fixed draw
workbook.prompt: Trace u=0.7 at T=1 and T=0.5. Does the different output demonstrate improved factual accuracy?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: T=1 selects blue; T=0.5 selects red. This follows changed intervals and supplies no factual correctness evidence.

workbook.title: Sample a new table independently
workbook.prompt: Probabilities A=0.5,B=0.3,C=0.2 in that order. Compute T=0.5 probabilities and cumulative boundaries. Trace u=0.5 and u=0.9 under T=1 and T=0.5. Explain the limit of the comparison.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Squared weights 0.25,0.09,0.04 total 0.38. Probabilities 25/38,9/38,4/38; boundaries 25/38 and 34/38. T=1: 0.5 selects B,0.9 selects C. T=0.5: 0.5 selects A,0.9 selects C because 0.9 > 34/38. The trace shows distribution effects, not factual accuracy.

workbook.title: Specify a valid experiment
workbook.prompt: A student changes the prompt and model as well as temperature, then attributes a better answer to temperature. Propose a fair comparison and reject any unsupported universal claim.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Fix prefix/prompt, model/version, candidate distribution and sampling policy while varying temperature. Record draws and evaluate stated task criteria across cases. The mixed comparison cannot isolate temperature; even a controlled result cannot prove all future outputs correct.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. All model outputs and probability tables are constructed classroom examples. No hosted AI service, external API or student account is needed. Distinguish a model objective from factual support and system permissions. Collect independent work before discussing its solutions.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Prepare the independent task and fresh retry without displaying solutions
sessions: Retrieve the prerequisite and distinguish a numerical claim from its interpretation.
Read section 1 and complete W1; ask for a reason alongside each answer.
Trace the worked case in section 2 and complete W2.
Discuss the diagram and complete W3 in pairs; record support.
Complete the guided response before sharing the answer.
Read the remaining sections and trace another constructed case.
Collect W4 independently, requiring calculations and a bounded conclusion.
Discuss W5 and the exit response. Provide feedback and a fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: T=1 gives red,blue,green; T=0.5 gives red,red,blue. Three fixed draws check the procedure, not expected long-run proportions. Exit: concentration changed; the claim of impossible factual errors lacks source-grounded evaluation and cannot be established by temperature alone.
misconceptions: Intervals have widths equal to the probabilities; unequal widths give unequal chances.
T=0 can be inserted into p^(1/T)
The formula requires T>0; greedy is a separate policy.
A probability transformation does not add factual evidence.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires probabilities 25/38,9/38,4/38, correct boundaries and B/C versus A/C. Fresh retry: A=0.4,B=0.4,C=0.2; at T=0.5 probabilities 4/9,4/9,1/9. Draws 0.4 and 0.85 select B,C at T=1 but A,B at T=0.5. Greedy ties must use an explicit rule.
teacher.support: Provide labelled intermediate columns and allow a calculator. Ask students to state the meaning and denominator of a value before interpreting it. Extension: implement the classroom calculation locally and test boundary cases without using personal data.
teacher.next: Week 5 connects token IDs to embedding vectors and introduces position information without treating IDs as semantic measurements.
